title: Epic of Gilgamesh, Old Babylonian version: the Yale tablet (Gilgamesh and Enkidu plan the journey to the Forest of Cedar)
source: Yale Peabody Museum tablet photographs + eBL manuscript transliterations (eBL corpus edition L I.4, Poem of Gilgamesh (ed. A. R. George, rev. G. Rozzi and E. Jiménez), OB III) + English of the eBL edition (A. R. George (eBL edition))
description: The Old Babylonian 'Yale tablet' of the Epic of Gilgamesh (YBC 2178, c. 18th century BCE): 218 of 219 lines, each shown on the Yale Peabody Museum photographs, with the eBL transliteration and A. R. George's English translation.
introduction:
The 'Yale tablet' (Yale Babylonian Collection YBC 2178, now YPM BC 016806) is one of the two large Old Babylonian tablets of the epic, written about a thousand years before the Nineveh copies. It is the third tablet of the Old Babylonian series that began 'Surpassing all other kings'. It tells how Gilgamesh and Enkidu, now friends, decide to go to the Forest of Cedar to kill Humbaba, how Enkidu and the elders of Uruk try to dissuade Gilgamesh, how weapons are cast for the journey, and how the heroes set out. It was first published by M. Jastrow and A. T. Clay in 1920. Its six columns (three on each face) and two short columns on the left edge are badly worn in places.

This page follows the line numbering of the eBL edition of the Old Babylonian Gilgamesh (ed. A. R. George). The photographs are the Yale Peabody Museum's, released as CC0.

How this page is built. Each section is a run of consecutive lines as written on one photographed clay tablet. For every line the eBL edition (https://www.ebl.lmu.de/corpus/L/1/4/OB/III) lists the manuscripts that carry it, with each tablet's own column and line numbers; the tablet chosen for each run is the photographed copy of the work with the most signs preserved there. Commentaries and texts that only quote a line are never chosen. School and excerpt tablets are used only for lines that no photographed library copy preserves as well, and only where they carry the line as text; their sections say so. The original text is eBL's transliteration of that tablet's signs (not a modern composite text): square brackets mark broken signs, x an illegible sign, # a damaged sign, ? an uncertain reading, and words in {braces} are determinatives; the notes give a key to every sign used on this page, and eBL's layout codes are written out in words (for example '(line break)' or '(blank space)'). Superscript numbers are the line numbers of the eBL edition, used in both the Akkadian and the English. The English is A. R. George's translation in the eBL edition (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0), one line of English per line of the poem; italics mark uncertain renderings, as in the source. Where the tablet is broken, the English still translates the whole line of eBL's composite text; each section's note names the lines that are broken on its tablet.

Finding a line on the photograph. Each section names the tablet, the face and column, and the tablet's own line numbers (a prime, as in 5', counts from the first preserved line of a broken column). On a tablet with six columns the obverse carries columns i-iii from left to right; the reverse, turned over from bottom to top, carries columns iv-vi from right to left. The photographs often show the obverse above the reverse with the edges around them; a fragment preserves only part of this layout.

This page shows 218 of the 219 lines of the eBL edition (100%), from 1 tablet in the Yale Peabody Museum: YBC.2178.

Lines not shown. 1 of the 219 lines of the eBL edition are not shown, because no photographed copy of the work used here carries them: 295 (no manuscript preserves it). A line is shown only on a photographed tablet that carries it as text. Commentaries and other texts that quote a line (letters, rituals, god lists) are not used as witnesses, because they carry it with explanations or inside another text; tablets without a photograph in eBL are not used, because the line could not be shown on its tablet.
translator_notes: Akkadian: eBL transliteration of the signs on the photographed tablet (manuscript-level ATF), not a composite text.
English: A. R. George's translation in the eBL edition; it renders eBL's composite text, including restorations from other tablets.
Line numbers: eBL edition (based on A. R. George, The Babylonian Gilgamesh Epic, Oxford 2003). Each section also gives the tablet's own column and line numbers.

Signs in the Akkadian: [ ] broken away; x illegible sign; # damaged sign; ? uncertain reading; ! sign corrected by the editor; ... broken signs of unknown number; ( ) signs perhaps broken away; { } determinative; << >> sign written in error by the scribe; (line break) the line runs on to the next line of the tablet.

136In order to safeguard [the cedar,]

138Gilgameš opened his mouth,
139saying to Enkidu:
140‘Who is there, my friend, that can climb to the sky?
141Only the gods have [dwelled] forever in sunlight.
142As for man, his days are numbered,
143whatever he may do, it is but wind.
144Here are you, afraid of death!
145For what purpose is the strength of your valour?
146I will walk in front of you,
147you can call to me, “Go to, do not fear!”
148If I fall, I should have made my name:
149-150(men will say) “Gilgameš joined battle with ferocious Ḫuwawa!”
151You were born and grew up in the wild,
152a lion attacked you and you experienced all.
153Grown men fled from your presence,
154-155[the] evening [star] even… you.
156[But (now)] you speak like a weakling,
157[with your] feeble [talk] you have vexed my heart.
158-159Let me start work and chop down the cedar!

162[let] them cast [hatchets] in our presence!’

182I will see the god of whom they speak,
183whose name the lands do constantly repeat.
184I will conquer him in the Forest of Cedar,
185-186that Uruk’s offshoot is mighty I will have the land learn.
187Let me start work and chop down the cedar,
188a name that is eternal I will establish for ever!’
189The elders of Uruk-the-City
190gave answer to Gilgameš:
191‘You are young, Gilgameš, and carried away by enthusiasm,
192whatever you do, you cannot understand.
193We hear of Ḫuwawa, (that) he is strange of visage:
194who is there can withstand his weapons?
195For sixty [leagues] the forest is a wilderness;
196who is there can venture inside it?
197Ḫuwawa, his voice is the Deluge,
198his speech is fire and his breath is death.
199Why do you desire to do this thing?
200An unwinnable battle is the ambush of Huwāwa.’
201Gilgameš heard the speech of his advisers,
202he looked at his friend and laughed:
203‘Now, my friend, how [I am frightened!]

254all the tricks of Huwawa.
255“The one who went in front kept his comrade safe;
256the one whose eyes were peeled [protected] himself!”
257May Šamaš allow you to achieve your ambition,
258may your eyes show (you) what you have talked of!
259May he open for you the paths that are shut,
260may he ready the road for your footsteps!
261May he ready the mountain for your feet,
262-263amay each night bring you a thing you will be glad of!
263b-264May Lugalbanda assist you in your victory;
265attain your desire like a little child!
266In Huwawa’s river, for which you are aiming,
267wash your feet!
268When you camp for the night, dig a well;
269in your bottle should be fresh water always.
270You must pour cool water (in libation) to Šamaš,
271you must remember your [god,] Lugalbanda.’
272Enkidu opened his mouth, saying to Gilgameš:
273‘Where you are minded begin the journey,
274[let] your heart [have no] fear, keep your eyes on me!
275[In the] forest I knew his lair,
276[and the ways] that Ḫuwawa wandered.
277Speak [to the crowd] and send them home!’
